M3 · Angular Momentum Algebra

Learning goals. After this chapter you should be able to

  • derive the spectrum of angular momentum from the commutation relations, and build the matrices of
    J\mathbf JJ for any jjj;
  • describe orbital angular momentum, parity and spin ½, including the sign change of a spinor under a
    rotation by 2π2\pi2π;
  • couple two angular momenta with Clebsch–Gordan coefficients and 3j symbols, and explain their
    semiclassical meaning;
  • explain how the spin–orbit interaction splits single-particle levels and produces the nuclear magic
    numbers;
  • rotate states and operators with Wigner DDD-matrices, and describe a deformed nucleus in the
    laboratory frame;
  • reduce matrix elements of tensor operators with the Wigner–Eckart theorem, and use it for
    quadrupole moments and B(E2)B(E2)B(E2) values;
  • recouple three and four angular momenta with 6j and 9j symbols, and compute the coupling matrix of
    a deformed potential;
  • list the coupled channels of a reaction for a given total JπJ^\piJπ.

Prerequisites: M1 (spherical harmonics and
Legendre polynomials). A first course in quantum mechanics helps but is not required.

Sources: C&H §6.1 (collisions of particles with spin) and §9.3 (partial-wave expansions with spin
in coupled channels); Thompson (1988), Appendix A (notation and phase conventions); Edmonds (1957) and
Brink & Satchler (1993) for the formulas of angular-momentum algebra; Bohr & Mottelson, Vol. I, for
the single-particle potential. Longer derivations are collected in the section Detailed derivation
at the end of the chapter.

How to read this chapter. Scattering problems with spins or with excited states of the nuclei
are bookkeeping problems in angular momentum. This chapter collects the tools: Sections M3.1–M3.4
build them, M3.5–M3.7 apply them to single-particle levels and deformed nuclei, and M3.8–M3.9
assemble the coupled-channel basis of Chapters 6, 9 and 14. The notebook checks every formula
against exact values from sympy or by brute-force sums, and the tools live in scatlib.angmom.

M3.1 Angular momentum operators and eigenstates

In M1 the quantization of orbital angular momentum came from a differential equation: the wave
function had to be finite on the sphere. That route is closed for spin, which has no wave function in
space, and it would be clumsy for the coupled states of several particles. Fortunately the whole
theory follows from the commutation relations alone. Any three operators JxJ_xJx​, JyJ_yJy​, JzJ_zJz​ that obey

[Jx,Jy]=iℏJz,[Jy,Jz]=iℏJx,[Jz,Jx]=iℏJy(M3.1)[J_x, J_y] = i\hbar J_z,\qquad [J_y, J_z] = i\hbar J_x,\qquad [J_z, J_x] = i\hbar J_y \tag{M3.1} [Jx​,Jy​]=iℏJz​,[Jy​,Jz​]=iℏJx​,[Jz​,Jx​]=iℏJy​(M3.1)

are an angular momentum: orbital angular momentum L=r×p\mathbf L = \mathbf r\times\mathbf pL=r×p, spin, and
their sums. For L\mathbf LL the relations follow from [x,px]=iℏ[x, p_x] = i\hbar[x,px​]=iℏ; for instance
[Lx,Ly]=[ypz−zpy, zpx−xpz]=iℏ(xpy−ypx)=iℏLz[L_x, L_y] = [yp_z - zp_y,\ zp_x - xp_z] = i\hbar(xp_y - yp_x) = i\hbar L_z[Lx​,Ly​]=[ypz​−zpy​, zpx​−xpz​]=iℏ(xpy​−ypx​)=iℏLz​. They express the fact that
rotations about different axes do not commute, and they are the defining property of every angular
momentum. From here on we set ℏ=1\hbar = 1ℏ=1 in angular-momentum algebra.

The spectrum follows in a few steps. J2\mathbf J^2J2 commutes with every component; for example
[Jx2,Jz]=−i(JxJy+JyJx)[J_x^2, J_z] = -i(J_xJ_y + J_yJ_x)[Jx2​,Jz​]=−i(Jx​Jy​+Jy​Jx​) and [Jy2,Jz]=+i(JyJx+JxJy)[J_y^2, J_z] = +i(J_yJ_x + J_xJ_y)[Jy2​,Jz​]=+i(Jy​Jx​+Jx​Jy​) cancel. So J2\mathbf J^2J2 and JzJ_zJz​
have common eigenstates, which we call ∣λm⟩|\lambda m\rangle∣λm⟩. Define the ladder operators
J±=Jx±iJyJ_\pm = J_x \pm iJ_yJ±​=Jx​±iJy​. By (M3.1), [Jz,J±]=iJy±Jx=±J±[J_z, J_\pm] = iJ_y \pm J_x = \pm J_\pm[Jz​,J±​]=iJy​±Jx​=±J±​, so
JzJ±∣λm⟩=J±(Jz±1)∣λm⟩=(m±1) J±∣λm⟩J_zJ_\pm|\lambda m\rangle = J_\pm(J_z \pm 1)|\lambda m\rangle = (m \pm 1)\,J_\pm|\lambda m\rangleJz​J±​∣λm⟩=J±​(Jz​±1)∣λm⟩=(m±1)J±​∣λm⟩: J±J_\pmJ±​ raises or
lowers the eigenvalue of JzJ_zJz​ by one and, since it commutes with J2\mathbf J^2J2, leaves λ\lambdaλ alone.
The ladder cannot go on forever. Multiplying out,
J∓J±=Jx2+Jy2±i[Jx,Jy]=J2−Jz2∓JzJ_\mp J_\pm = J_x^2 + J_y^2 \pm i[J_x, J_y] = \mathbf J^2 - J_z^2 \mp J_zJ∓​J±​=Jx2​+Jy2​±i[Jx​,Jy​]=J2−Jz2​∓Jz​, so the squared norm of
J±∣λm⟩J_\pm|\lambda m\rangleJ±​∣λm⟩ is

∥J±∣λm⟩∥2=⟨λm∣J∓J±∣λm⟩=λ−m(m±1),\big\|J_\pm|\lambda m\rangle\big\|^2 = \langle\lambda m|J_\mp J_\pm|\lambda m\rangle = \lambda - m(m \pm 1), ∥∥∥​J±​∣λm⟩∥∥∥​2=⟨λm∣J∓​J±​∣λm⟩=λ−m(m±1),

which cannot be negative. The ladder must therefore stop at both ends, with J+J_+J+​ annihilating the top
state and J−J_-J−​ the bottom one. If jjj is the largest mmm, then J+∣λj⟩=0J_+|\lambda j\rangle = 0J+​∣λj⟩=0 requires
λ=j(j+1)\lambda = j(j+1)λ=j(j+1). If j′j'j′ is the smallest, J−∣λj′⟩=0J_-|\lambda j'\rangle = 0J−​∣λj′⟩=0 requires λ=j′(j′−1)\lambda = j'(j' - 1)λ=j′(j′−1), whose
root below jjj is j′=−jj' = -jj′=−j. Going from jjj to −j-j−j in integer steps requires 2j2j2j to be an integer.
Hence

J2∣jm⟩=j(j+1) ∣jm⟩,Jz∣jm⟩=m ∣jm⟩,j=0,12,1,32,…,m=−j,−j+1,…,j,(M3.2)\mathbf J^2|jm\rangle = j(j+1)\,|jm\rangle,\qquad J_z|jm\rangle = m\,|jm\rangle,\qquad j = 0, \tfrac12, 1, \tfrac32, \dots,\quad m = -j, -j+1, \dots, j , \tag{M3.2} J2∣jm⟩=j(j+1)∣jm⟩,Jz​∣jm⟩=m∣jm⟩,j=0,21​,1,23​,…,m=−j,−j+1,…,j,(M3.2)

and the ladder operators act as

J±∣jm⟩=j(j+1)−m(m±1)  ∣j,m±1⟩.(M3.3)J_\pm|jm\rangle = \sqrt{j(j+1) - m(m\pm1)}\;|j,m\pm1\rangle . \tag{M3.3} J±​∣jm⟩=j(j+1)−m(m±1)​∣j,m±1⟩.(M3.3)

The square root is the norm computed above, with λ=j(j+1)\lambda = j(j+1)λ=j(j+1); only its phase is a matter of
choice. Taking it real and positive is the Condon–Shortley convention, used everywhere in these
notes. Equation (M3.3) gives the matrices of Jx=(J++J−)/2J_x = (J_+ + J_-)/2Jx​=(J+​+J−​)/2 and Jy=(J+−J−)/2iJ_y = (J_+ - J_-)/2iJy​=(J+​−J−​)/2i for any jjj;
scatlib.angmom.jmatrices builds them, and the notebook confirms (M3.1) and (M3.2) to 10−1410^{-14}10−14 for jjj
up to 15/215/215/2.

The same algebra shows that an angular momentum can never point exactly along an axis. In the state
∣jm⟩|jm\rangle∣jm⟩ the terms J+2J_+^2J+2​ and J−2J_-^2J−2​ in Jx2=(J++J−)2/4J_x^2 = (J_+ + J_-)^2/4Jx2​=(J+​+J−​)2/4 have no diagonal matrix elements, so
⟨Jx2⟩=14⟨J+J−+J−J+⟩\langle J_x^2\rangle = \frac14\langle J_+J_- + J_-J_+\rangle⟨Jx2​⟩=41​⟨J+​J−​+J−​J+​⟩, and the norms above give

⟨Jx2⟩=⟨Jy2⟩=12[j(j+1)−m2]>0.(M3.4)\langle J_x^2\rangle = \langle J_y^2\rangle = \tfrac12\big[j(j+1) - m^2\big] > 0 . \tag{M3.4} ⟨Jx2​⟩=⟨Jy2​⟩=21​[j(j+1)−m2]>0.(M3.4)

Even for m=jm = jm=j the transverse components do not vanish. Semiclassically, J\mathbf JJ has length
j(j+1)\sqrt{j(j+1)}j(j+1)​ and lies on a cone about the zzz axis with cos⁡θ=m/j(j+1)\cos\theta = m/\sqrt{j(j+1)}cosθ=m/j(j+1)​; for j=2j = 2j=2,
m=2m = 2m=2 the half-angle of the cone is 35.3°. This picture will explain the Clebsch–Gordan coefficients
in §M3.4.

M3.2 Orbital angular momentum and parity

For orbital angular momentum the abstract states ∣lm⟩|lm\rangle∣lm⟩ become functions on the sphere. In
spherical coordinates Lz=−i ∂/∂ϕL_z = -i\,\partial/\partial\phiLz​=−i∂/∂ϕ, L2\mathbf L^2L2 is the angular part of the
Laplacian (M1.2), and converting L=−i r×∇\mathbf L = -i\,\mathbf r\times\nablaL=−ir×∇ to spherical coordinates gives
the ladder operators

L±=e±iϕ(±∂∂θ+icot⁡θ ∂∂ϕ),(M3.5)L_\pm = e^{\pm i\phi}\left(\pm\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta} + i\cot\theta\,\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi}\right), \tag{M3.5} L±​=e±iϕ(±∂θ∂​+icotθ∂ϕ∂​),(M3.5)

and the eigenfunctions are the spherical harmonics Ylm(θ,ϕ)Y_{lm}(\theta, \phi)Ylm​(θ,ϕ) of M1. As a check,
L+Yll=0L_+Y_{ll} = 0L+​Yll​=0: with Yll∝sin⁡lθ eilϕY_{ll} \propto \sin^l\theta\,e^{il\phi}Yll​∝sinlθeilϕ, the derivative ∂θ\partial_\theta∂θ​ gives
lcos⁡θsin⁡l−1θ eilϕl\cos\theta\sin^{l-1}\theta\,e^{il\phi}lcosθsinl−1θeilϕ, and icot⁡θ ∂ϕi\cot\theta\,\partial_\phiicotθ∂ϕ​ gives exactly the negative of this.
A wave function must be single valued, so eimϕe^{im\phi}eimϕ forces integer mmm, and therefore integer lll.
Half-integer angular momenta exist only as spin.

Besides angular momentum, the spherical harmonics carry a second quantum number that matters in every
reaction: parity. The parity operator maps r→−r\mathbf r \to -\mathbf rr→−r, that is θ→π−θ\theta \to \pi - \thetaθ→π−θ and
ϕ→ϕ+π\phi \to \phi + \piϕ→ϕ+π. As shown in M1 §M1.2, PlmP_l^mPlm​ then picks up the factor (−1)l+m(-1)^{l+m}(−1)l+m and eimϕe^{im\phi}eimϕ the
factor (−1)m(-1)^m(−1)m, so

Ylm(π−θ,ϕ+π)=(−1)l Ylm(θ,ϕ),(M3.6)Y_{lm}(\pi - \theta, \phi + \pi) = (-1)^l\,Y_{lm}(\theta, \phi), \tag{M3.6} Ylm​(π−θ,ϕ+π)=(−1)lYlm​(θ,ϕ),(M3.6)

which the notebook confirms to 4×10−154\times10^{-15}4×10−15 for l≤5l \le 5l≤5. A partial wave lll has parity
(−1)l(-1)^l(−1)l. In a central potential both lll and parity are conserved. In a non-central one, such as the
potential of a deformed nucleus or the tensor force, only the total angular momentum and the parity
survive. That is why reaction channels are labelled by JπJ^\piJπ (§M3.9).

(∝cos⁡mϕ\propto\cos m\phi∝cosmϕ) for l≤3l \le 3l≤3, drawn as surfaces at distance ∣Y∣|Y|∣Y∣ from the origin and coloured

M3.3 Spin one-half

The smallest non-trivial case of (M3.2), j=12j = \frac12j=21​, has no orbital counterpart; it describes the
spin of nucleons and electrons. There are two states, m=±12m = \pm\frac12m=±21​, and (M3.3) gives
J+∣−12⟩=∣12⟩J_+|{-\tfrac12}\rangle = |\tfrac12\rangleJ+​∣−21​⟩=∣21​⟩ and J−∣12⟩=∣−12⟩J_-|\tfrac12\rangle = |{-\tfrac12}\rangleJ−​∣21​⟩=∣−21​⟩, both with the
coefficient 34+14=1\sqrt{\frac34 + \frac14} = 143​+41​​=1. In the basis (m=+12,−12)(m = +\frac12, -\frac12)(m=+21​,−21​) this means
J+=(0100)J_+ = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}J+​=(00​10​), J−=(0010)J_- = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}J−​=(01​00​) and
Jz=diag(12,−12)J_z = \mathrm{diag}(\frac12, -\frac12)Jz​=diag(21​,−21​). Then Jx=(J++J−)/2J_x = (J_+ + J_-)/2Jx​=(J+​+J−​)/2 and Jy=(J+−J−)/2iJ_y = (J_+ - J_-)/2iJy​=(J+​−J−​)/2i are one half of
the Pauli matrices, and the spin is S=σ/2\mathbf S = \boldsymbol\sigma/2S=σ/2 with

σx=(0110),σy=(0−ii0),σz=(100−1),σiσj=δij+i ϵijk σk.(M3.7)\sigma_x = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y = \begin{pmatrix}0 & -i\\ i & 0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_i\sigma_j = \delta_{ij} + i\,\epsilon_{ijk}\,\sigma_k . \tag{M3.7} σx​=(01​10​),σy​=(0i​−i0​),σz​=(10​0−1​),σi​σj​=δij​+iϵijk​σk​.(M3.7)

The product rule can be checked by direct multiplication; for example σxσy=iσz\sigma_x\sigma_y = i\sigma_zσx​σy​=iσz​.
(scatlib orders the basis by increasing mmm, so its matrices appear with rows and columns reversed.)

Rotations of a spinor are especially simple. The product rule gives
(σ⋅n^)2=ninj(δij+iϵijkσk)=1(\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n})^2 = n_in_j(\delta_{ij} + i\epsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k) = 1(σ⋅n^)2=ni​nj​(δij​+iϵijk​σk​)=1, because the
antisymmetric ϵijk\epsilon_{ijk}ϵijk​ vanishes against the symmetric ninjn_in_jni​nj​. In the power series of the
exponential, the even powers of σ⋅n^\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}σ⋅n^ are therefore 1 and the odd powers are
σ⋅n^\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}σ⋅n^, and a rotation by β\betaβ about the axis n^\hat{\mathbf n}n^ is

e−iβ σ⋅n^/2=cos⁡β2−i σ⋅n^ sin⁡β2.(M3.8)e^{-i\beta\,\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}/2} = \cos\frac{\beta}{2} - i\,\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,\sin\frac{\beta}{2} . \tag{M3.8} e−iβσ⋅n^/2=cos2β​−iσ⋅n^sin2β​.(M3.8)

At β=2π\beta = 2\piβ=2π this is −1-1−1. A spinor changes sign under a full turn and returns to itself only
after 4π4\pi4π (Fig. M3.4a). Observables are bilinear in the spinor and do not notice. But the sign is
real. In neutron interferometry, one of two coherent beams has its spin precessed in a magnetic field.
The interference pattern is shifted by half a period after a precession of 2π2\pi2π, and repeats only
after 4π4\pi4π (Rauch et al. 1975; Werner et al. 1975).

The state “spin up along n^\hat{\mathbf n}n^”, with polar angles (θ,ϕ)(\theta, \phi)(θ,ϕ), is the eigenvector of
σ⋅n^\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}σ⋅n^ with eigenvalue +1+1+1,
χ=(cos⁡θ2, eiϕsin⁡θ2)\chi = \big(\cos\frac\theta2,\ e^{i\phi}\sin\frac\theta2\big)χ=(cos2θ​, eiϕsin2θ​), as the half-angle formulas confirm with
σ⋅n^=(cos⁡θe−iϕsin⁡θeiϕsin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf n} = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & e^{-i\phi}\sin\theta\\ e^{i\phi}\sin\theta & -\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}σ⋅n^=(cosθeiϕsinθ​e−iϕsinθ−cosθ​).
Its ⟨σ⟩\langle\boldsymbol\sigma\rangle⟨σ⟩ is n^\hat{\mathbf n}n^; for instance
⟨σz⟩=cos⁡2θ2−sin⁡2θ2=cos⁡θ\langle\sigma_z\rangle = \cos^2\frac\theta2 - \sin^2\frac\theta2 = \cos\theta⟨σz​⟩=cos22θ​−sin22θ​=cosθ. Conversely, any normalized
two-component spinor takes this form once an overall phase is removed, so every spin-½ state is spin
up along some direction. That is why the polarization of a spin-½ beam is described by a single vector
(Chapter 6).

M3.4 Coupling two angular momenta

Two angular momenta j1\mathbf j_1j1​ and j2\mathbf j_2j2​ acting on different degrees of freedom (orbit and
spin, or two particles) commute, and their sum J=j1+j2\mathbf J = \mathbf j_1 + \mathbf j_2J=j1​+j2​ is again an
angular momentum. Two bases describe the same (2j1+1)(2j2+1)(2j_1+1)(2j_2+1)(2j1​+1)(2j2​+1) states: the product basis
∣j1m1⟩∣j2m2⟩|j_1m_1\rangle|j_2m_2\rangle∣j1​m1​⟩∣j2​m2​⟩, with j1zj_{1z}j1z​ and j2zj_{2z}j2z​ diagonal, and the coupled basis
∣j1j2;JM⟩|j_1j_2;JM\rangle∣j1​j2​;JM⟩, with J2\mathbf J^2J2 and JzJ_zJz​ diagonal. The Clebsch–Gordan coefficients
connect them:

∣j1j2;JM⟩=∑m1m2⟨j1m1j2m2∣JM⟩ ∣j1m1⟩∣j2m2⟩.(M3.9)|j_1j_2;JM\rangle = \sum_{m_1m_2}\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|JM\rangle\,|j_1m_1\rangle|j_2m_2\rangle . \tag{M3.9} ∣j1​j2​;JM⟩=m1​m2​∑​⟨j1​m1​j2​m2​∣JM⟩∣j1​m1​⟩∣j2​m2​⟩.(M3.9)

Since Jz=j1z+j2zJ_z = j_{1z} + j_{2z}Jz​=j1z​+j2z​ is diagonal in both bases, the coefficients vanish unless M=m1+m2M = m_1 + m_2M=m1​+m2​.
They also vanish unless JJJ obeys the triangle rule ∣j1−j2∣≤J≤j1+j2|j_1 - j_2| \le J \le j_1 + j_2∣j1​−j2​∣≤J≤j1​+j2​, which a count of
states explains. The largest MMM, j1+j2j_1 + j_2j1​+j2​, is reached only by the stretched product state, so the
largest JJJ is j1+j2j_1 + j_2j1​+j2​. One unit lower there are two product states (if neither angular momentum is
zero), but only one combination belongs to J=j1+j2J = j_1 + j_2J=j1​+j2​, so a new multiplet J=j1+j2−1J = j_1 + j_2 - 1J=j1​+j2​−1 must
begin. Each further step down in
MMM adds one product state, and with it one new multiplet, until the number of product states stops
growing at M=∣j1−j2∣M = |j_1 - j_2|M=∣j1​−j2​∣. The count works: ∑J(2J+1)=(2j1+1)(2j2+1)\sum_J(2J+1) = (2j_1+1)(2j_2+1)∑J​(2J+1)=(2j1​+1)(2j2​+1).

The coefficients can be constructed with the ladder operators alone. Start from the stretched state,
∣J=j1+j2,M=J⟩=∣j1j1⟩∣j2j2⟩|J = j_1+j_2, M = J\rangle = |j_1j_1\rangle|j_2j_2\rangle∣J=j1​+j2​,M=J⟩=∣j1​j1​⟩∣j2​j2​⟩. Apply J−=j1−+j2−J_- = j_{1-} + j_{2-}J−​=j1−​+j2−​ with (M3.3) to obtain
the other members of that multiplet. The state with M=j1+j2−1M = j_1 + j_2 - 1M=j1​+j2​−1 orthogonal to them starts the
multiplet J=j1+j2−1J = j_1 + j_2 - 1J=j1​+j2​−1, and so on. The simplest example is two spins ½. The stretched state is
∣1,1⟩=∣↑↑⟩|1, 1\rangle = |{\uparrow\uparrow}\rangle∣1,1⟩=∣↑↑⟩. Applying J−J_-J−​, the left side gives 2 ∣1,0⟩\sqrt2\,|1, 0\rangle2​∣1,0⟩ by (M3.3) and
the right side gives ∣↓↑⟩+∣↑↓⟩|{\downarrow\uparrow}\rangle + |{\uparrow\downarrow}\rangle∣↓↑⟩+∣↑↓⟩, so
∣1,0⟩=(∣↑↓⟩+∣↓↑⟩)/2|1, 0\rangle = (|{\uparrow\downarrow}\rangle + |{\downarrow\uparrow}\rangle)/\sqrt2∣1,0⟩=(∣↑↓⟩+∣↓↑⟩)/2​, and one more step gives
∣1,−1⟩=∣↓↓⟩|1, -1\rangle = |{\downarrow\downarrow}\rangle∣1,−1⟩=∣↓↓⟩. The combination of the two M=0M = 0M=0 product states orthogonal to
∣1,0⟩|1, 0\rangle∣1,0⟩ is the singlet ∣0,0⟩=(∣↑↓⟩−∣↓↑⟩)/2|0, 0\rangle = (|{\uparrow\downarrow}\rangle - |{\downarrow\uparrow}\rangle)/\sqrt2∣0,0⟩=(∣↑↓⟩−∣↓↑⟩)/2​. These
three symmetric triplet states and one antisymmetric singlet state are the spin states of two nucleons:
the triplet of the deuteron, and the singlet that dominates low-energy neutron–proton scattering
(Chapter 2). The overall sign of each new multiplet is a convention. With the choice
⟨j1j1 j2(J−j1)∣JJ⟩>0\langle j_1j_1\,j_2(J - j_1)|JJ\rangle > 0⟨j1​j1​j2​(J−j1​)∣JJ⟩>0, all coefficients are real.

For l=1l = 1l=1 coupled to spin ½ (a ppp orbit) the same steps give the exact values that the notebook
prints:

Both bases are orthonormal, so the coefficients form a real orthogonal matrix:

∑m1m2⟨j1m1j2m2∣JM⟩⟨j1m1j2m2∣J′M′⟩=δJJ′δMM′,∑JM⟨j1m1j2m2∣JM⟩⟨j1m1′j2m2′∣JM⟩=δm1m1′δm2m2′.(M3.11)\sum_{m_1m_2}\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|JM\rangle\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|J'M'\rangle = \delta_{JJ'}\delta_{MM'},\qquad \sum_{JM}\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|JM\rangle\langle j_1m_1'j_2m_2'|JM\rangle = \delta_{m_1m_1'}\delta_{m_2m_2'} . \tag{M3.11} m1​m2​∑​⟨j1​m1​j2​m2​∣JM⟩⟨j1​m1​j2​m2​∣J′M′⟩=δJJ′​δMM′​,JM∑​⟨j1​m1​j2​m2​∣JM⟩⟨j1​m1′​j2​m2′​∣JM⟩=δm1​m1′​​δm2​m2′​​.(M3.11)

For calculations and tables, the coefficients are usually written as Wigner 3j symbols, which have

⟨j1m1j2m2∣JM⟩=(−1)j1−j2+M2J+1(j1j2Jm1m2−M).(M3.12)\langle j_1m_1j_2m_2|JM\rangle = (-1)^{j_1 - j_2 + M}\sqrt{2J+1}\begin{pmatrix}j_1 & j_2 & J\\ m_1 & m_2 & -M\end{pmatrix}. \tag{M3.12} ⟨j1​m1​j2​m2​∣JM⟩=(−1)j1​−j2​+M2J+1​(j1​m1​​j2​m2​​J−M​).(M3.12)

M3.5 Spin–orbit coupling

The first physical application is the coupling of a nucleon’s spin to its orbit. A spin-½ particle in
an orbit lll has the coupled states ∣(l12)jm⟩|(l\tfrac12)jm\rangle∣(l21​)jm⟩ with j=l±12j = l \pm \frac12j=l±21​. Their angular parts are
the spin-angle functions

Yjml=∑ms=±1/2⟨l, m−ms, 12, ms∣jm⟩  Yl,m−ms(r^) χms.(M3.15)\mathcal Y^{l}_{jm} = \sum_{m_s = \pm1/2}\big\langle l,\,m - m_s,\,\tfrac12,\,m_s\big|jm\big\rangle\;Y_{l,m-m_s}(\hat{\mathbf r})\,\chi_{m_s} . \tag{M3.15} Yjml​=ms​=±1/2∑​⟨l,m−ms​,21​,ms​∣∣∣​jm⟩Yl,m−ms​​(r^)χms​​.(M3.15)

Because l\mathbf ll and s\mathbf ss act on different variables they commute, so
j2=(l+s)2=l2+s2+2 l⋅s\mathbf j^2 = (\mathbf l + \mathbf s)^2 = \mathbf l^2 + \mathbf s^2 + 2\,\mathbf l\cdot\mathbf sj2=(l+s)2=l2+s2+2l⋅s, and the operator
l⋅s=12(j2−l2−s2)\mathbf l\cdot\mathbf s = \frac12(\mathbf j^2 - \mathbf l^2 - \mathbf s^2)l⋅s=21​(j2−l2−s2) is diagonal in this basis:

⟨l⋅s⟩=12[j(j+1)−l(l+1)−34]={     l/2,j=l+12,−(l+1)/2,j=l−12.(M3.16)\langle\mathbf l\cdot\mathbf s\rangle = \tfrac12\big[j(j+1) - l(l+1) - \tfrac34\big] = \begin{cases} \;\;\,l/2, & j = l + \frac12,\\ -(l+1)/2, & j = l - \frac12 .\end{cases} \tag{M3.16} ⟨l⋅s⟩=21​[j(j+1)−l(l+1)−43​]={l/2,−(l+1)/2,​j=l+21​,j=l−21​.​(M3.16)

Inserting j=l+12j = l + \frac12j=l+21​ gives 12[(l+12)(l+32)−l(l+1)−34]=l/2\frac12[(l + \frac12)(l + \frac32) - l(l+1) - \frac34] = l/221​[(l+21​)(l+23​)−l(l+1)−43​]=l/2, and j=l−12j = l - \frac12j=l−21​
gives −(l+1)/2-(l+1)/2−(l+1)/2. A spin–orbit interaction therefore splits each orbit l>0l > 0l>0 into two levels, and the
splitting grows like l/2+(l+1)/2=(2l+1)/2l/2 + (l+1)/2 = (2l+1)/2l/2+(l+1)/2=(2l+1)/2.

In nuclei the spin–orbit force is strong, peaked at the surface, and of the opposite sign to the
atomic one: the level with j=l+12j = l + \frac12j=l+21​ lies lower. A standard single-particle potential (Bohr &
Mottelson) is

V(r)=V0 f(r)+Vls r02 1rdfdr ⟨l⋅s⟩,f(r)=11+e(r−R)/a,(M3.17)V(r) = V_0\,f(r) + V_{ls}\,r_0^2\,\frac{1}{r}\frac{df}{dr}\,\langle\mathbf l\cdot\mathbf s\rangle,\qquad f(r) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{(r - R)/a}}, \tag{M3.17} V(r)=V0​f(r)+Vls​r02​r1​drdf​⟨l⋅s⟩,f(r)=1+e(r−R)/a1​,(M3.17)

with V0=−51+33(N−Z)/AV_0 = -51 + 33(N - Z)/AV0​=−51+33(N−Z)/A MeV for neutrons, Vls=−0.44 V0V_{ls} = -0.44\,V_0Vls​=−0.44V0​, R=r0A1/3R = r_0A^{1/3}R=r0​A1/3,
r0=1.27r_0 = 1.27r0​=1.27 fm and a=0.67a = 0.67a=0.67 fm. The radial factor 1r df/dr\frac1r\,df/drr1​df/dr, the derivative of the density
profile, is what confines the force to the surface. Since df/dr<0df/dr < 0df/dr<0 and Vls>0V_{ls} > 0Vls​>0, the spin–orbit
term is attractive for j=l+12j = l + \frac12j=l+21​, where ⟨l⋅s⟩>0\langle\mathbf l\cdot\mathbf s\rangle > 0⟨l⋅s⟩>0. For the neutrons of
²⁰⁸Pb, (N−Z)/A=44/208(N - Z)/A = 44/208(N−Z)/A=44/208 gives V0=−44.02V_0 = -44.02V0​=−44.02 MeV, Vls=19.37V_{ls} = 19.37Vls​=19.37 MeV and R=7.525R = 7.525R=7.525 fm.

The notebook finds the bound levels of (M3.17) with the bound-state solver of Chapter 2, while the
spin–orbit strength is turned on from zero to its full value (Fig. M3.3 and Animation M3.2). Without
spin–orbit coupling, the wide gaps fall at N=2,8,20,40,58,92N = 2, 8, 20, 40, 58, 92N=2,8,20,40,58,92 and 138138138, with weaker ones at
18, 34, 70 and 112. These are the closed shells of a flat-bottomed well, and apart from 2, 8 and 20
they are not the observed magic numbers. With full spin–orbit coupling, the gaps fall at
N=2,8,20,28,50,82N = 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82N=2,8,20,28,50,82 and 126126126, with weaker ones at 40 and 100. The decisive levels are the
high-jjj partners 1f7/21f_{7/2}1f7/2​, 1g9/21g_{9/2}1g9/2​, 1h11/21h_{11/2}1h11/2​, 1i13/21i_{13/2}1i13/2​ and 1j15/21j_{15/2}1j15/2​. Their splitting
(2l+1)/2(2l+1)/2(2l+1)/2 grows with lll, so each is pulled down into the shell below, and each creates a new magic
number. This explanation of the magic numbers by Mayer and by Haxel, Jensen and Suess (1949)
established the nuclear shell model. Note also the 1j15/21j_{15/2}1j15/2​ level: it is not bound at all without
spin–orbit coupling and becomes bound only above about half strength.

The comparison with experiment is quantitative. The last occupied neutron orbit of ²⁰⁸Pb is
3p1/23p_{1/2}3p1/2​, and its energy is minus the neutron separation energy of ²⁰⁸Pb. The first empty orbit is
2g9/22g_{9/2}2g9/2​, whose energy is minus the separation energy of ²⁰⁹Pb. From the AME2020 masses,
Sn(208Pb)=7.368S_n(^{208}\mathrm{Pb}) = 7.368Sn​(208Pb)=7.368 MeV and Sn(209Pb)=3.937S_n(^{209}\mathrm{Pb}) = 3.937Sn​(209Pb)=3.937 MeV, so the N=126N = 126N=126 gap is
3.43 MeV. The potential gives E(3p1/2)=−7.18E(3p_{1/2}) = -7.18E(3p1/2​)=−7.18 MeV, E(2g9/2)=−3.62E(2g_{9/2}) = -3.62E(2g9/2​)=−3.62 MeV and a gap of
3.55 MeV.

The same surface-peaked form appears in reactions. In the optical potential it produces the
polarization of scattered nucleons (Chapter 6), and bound states of (M3.17) are the form factors of
transfer reactions (Chapters 11–12). Optical-model codes usually write the term in the Thomas form,
with (ℏ/mπc)2≈2.0(\hbar/m_\pi c)^2 \approx 2.0(ℏ/mπ​c)2≈2.0 fm² in place of r02r_0^2r02​, and often with
l⋅σ=2 l⋅s\mathbf l\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma = 2\,\mathbf l\cdot\mathbf sl⋅σ=2l⋅s. Equating the two forms,
Vso=Vls r02/(2×2.0 fm2)V_{so} = V_{ls}\,r_0^2/(2\times2.0\ \mathrm{fm}^2)Vso​=Vls​r02​/(2×2.0 fm2), so the strength above corresponds to
Vso≈7.8V_{so} \approx 7.8Vso​≈7.8 MeV, a typical optical-model value. Always check a code’s convention before copying
parameters; for FRESCO, see Thompson’s manual.

M3.6 Rotation matrices

Coupling combines angular momenta. The next tool describes how states change when the frame of
reference is rotated, which is needed whenever a nucleus is deformed, because its shape is simple
only in its own body-fixed frame. A rotation by the Euler angles (α,β,γ)(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)(α,β,γ) is: first
by γ\gammaγ about zzz, then by β\betaβ about yyy, then by α\alphaα about zzz. Since JnJ_nJn​ generates
rotations about the axis nnn, its operator is
R(α,β,γ)=e−iαJze−iβJye−iγJzR(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) = e^{-i\alpha J_z}e^{-i\beta J_y}e^{-i\gamma J_z}R(α,β,γ)=e−iαJz​e−iβJy​e−iγJz​. A rotation commutes with
J2\mathbf J^2J2, which is a scalar, so it never changes jjj and only mixes mmm:

R ∣jm⟩=∑m′∣jm′⟩ Dm′mj(α,β,γ),Dm′mj(α,β,γ)=e−im′α dm′mj(β) e−imγ.(M3.18)R\,|jm\rangle = \sum_{m'}|jm'\rangle\,D^j_{m'm}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma),\qquad D^j_{m'm}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) = e^{-im'\alpha}\,d^j_{m'm}(\beta)\,e^{-im\gamma} . \tag{M3.18} R∣jm⟩=m′∑​∣jm′⟩Dm′mj​(α,β,γ),Dm′mj​(α,β,γ)=e−im′αdm′mj​(β)e−imγ.(M3.18)

The factorization follows because JzJ_zJz​ is diagonal: the two outer exponentials only multiply by the
phases e−im′αe^{-im'\alpha}e−im′α and e−imγe^{-im\gamma}e−imγ. The reduced rotation matrices
dm′mj(β)=⟨jm′∣e−iβJy∣jm⟩d^j_{m'm}(\beta) = \langle jm'|e^{-i\beta J_y}|jm\rangledm′mj​(β)=⟨jm′∣e−iβJy​∣jm⟩ are real and given by Wigner’s formula:

dm′mj(β)=∑k(−1)k−m+m′(j+m)! (j−m)! (j+m′)! (j−m′)!(j+m−k)! k! (j−k−m′)! (k−m+m′)!(cos⁡β2)2j−2k+m−m′(sin⁡β2)2k−m+m′.(M3.19)d^j_{m'm}(\beta) = \sum_k\frac{(-1)^{k - m + m'}\sqrt{(j+m)!\,(j-m)!\,(j+m')!\,(j-m')!}} {(j + m - k)!\,k!\,(j - k - m')!\,(k - m + m')!} \left(\cos\frac\beta2\right)^{2j - 2k + m - m'}\left(\sin\frac\beta2\right)^{2k - m + m'} . \tag{M3.19} dm′mj​(β)=k∑​(j+m−k)!k!(j−k−m′)!(k−m+m′)!(−1)k−m+m′(j+m)!(j−m)!(j+m′)!(j−m′)!​​(cos2β​)2j−2k+m−m′(sin2β​)2k−m+m′.(M3.19)

For j=12j = \frac12j=21​ the matrix follows directly from (M3.8) with n^=y^\hat{\mathbf n} = \hat{\mathbf y}n^=y^​:
e−iβσy/2=cos⁡β2−iσysin⁡β2=(cos⁡β2−sin⁡β2sin⁡β2cos⁡β2)e^{-i\beta\sigma_y/2} = \cos\frac\beta2 - i\sigma_y\sin\frac\beta2 = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\frac\beta2 & -\sin\frac\beta2\\ \sin\frac\beta2 & \cos\frac\beta2\end{pmatrix}e−iβσy​/2=cos2β​−iσy​sin2β​=(cos2β​sin2β​​−sin2β​cos2β​​).
So d±1/2,±1/21/2=cos⁡β2d^{1/2}_{\pm1/2,\pm1/2} = \cos\frac\beta2d±1/2,±1/21/2​=cos2β​ and d±1/2,∓1/21/2=∓sin⁡β2d^{1/2}_{\pm1/2,\mp1/2} = \mp\sin\frac\beta2d±1/2,∓1/21/2​=∓sin2β​, which (M3.19)
reproduces. For larger jjj, one way to obtain (M3.19) is to build ∣jm⟩|jm\rangle∣jm⟩ from 2j2j2j spin-½ objects,
each of which rotates with d1/2d^{1/2}d1/2, and to collect the powers of cos⁡β2\cos\frac\beta2cos2β​ and sin⁡β2\sin\frac\beta2sin2β​
(Edmonds 1957, ch. 4).

The DDD-matrices are unitary and multiply like the rotations themselves,
Dj(R1) Dj(R2)=Dj(R1R2)D^j(R_1)\,D^j(R_2) = D^j(R_1R_2)Dj(R1​)Dj(R2​)=Dj(R1​R2​). Their symmetries include
dm′mj(β)=(−1)m−m′dmm′j(β)=d−m,−m′j(β)d^j_{m'm}(\beta) = (-1)^{m - m'}d^j_{mm'}(\beta) = d^j_{-m,-m'}(\beta)dm′mj​(β)=(−1)m−m′dmm′j​(β)=d−m,−m′j​(β). For integer j=lj = lj=l and m=0m = 0m=0,

M3.7 Tensor operators and the Wigner–Eckart theorem

States are not the only objects that transform under rotations; operators do too, and the most useful
operators transform in the simplest possible way. A spherical tensor operator of rank kkk is a set
of 2k+12k+12k+1 operators TqkT^k_qTqk​, q=−k,…,kq = -k, \dots, kq=−k,…,k, that rotate like the spherical harmonics YkqY_{kq}Ykq​:

R Tqk R†=∑q′Tq′k Dq′qk(R),equivalently[Jz,Tqk]=q Tqk,[J±,Tqk]=k(k+1)−q(q±1)  Tq±1k.(M3.23)R\,T^k_q\,R^\dagger = \sum_{q'}T^k_{q'}\,D^k_{q'q}(R),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad [J_z, T^k_q] = q\,T^k_q,\quad [J_\pm, T^k_q] = \sqrt{k(k+1) - q(q\pm1)}\;T^k_{q\pm1} . \tag{M3.23} RTqk​R†=q′∑​Tq′k​Dq′qk​(R),equivalently[Jz​,Tqk​]=qTqk​,[J±​,Tqk​]=k(k+1)−q(q±1)​Tq±1k​.(M3.23)

The second form is the first for an infinitesimal rotation R=1−iε n^⋅JR = 1 - i\varepsilon\,\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathbf JR=1−iεn^⋅J:
the left side becomes Tqk−iε[n^⋅J,Tqk]T^k_q - i\varepsilon[\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathbf J, T^k_q]Tqk​−iε[n^⋅J,Tqk​], and the right side contains
the matrix elements (M3.2) and (M3.3) of n^⋅J\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathbf Jn^⋅J for angular momentum kkk. Examples are
a scalar (k=0k = 0k=0), the spherical components of a vector, V±1=∓(Vx±iVy)/2V_{\pm1} = \mp(V_x \pm iV_y)/\sqrt2V±1​=∓(Vx​±iVy​)/2​ and
V0=VzV_0 = V_zV0​=Vz​ (k=1k = 1k=1), the functions Ykq(r^)Y_{kq}(\hat{\mathbf r})Ykq​(r^) themselves, the electric multipole operators
e rλYλμe\,r^\lambda Y_{\lambda\mu}erλYλμ​, and the quadrupole operator Q2μ=16π/5 r2Y2μQ_{2\mu} = \sqrt{16\pi/5}\,r^2Y_{2\mu}Q2μ​=16π/5​r2Y2μ​.

For such operators a remarkable simplification holds: the dependence of a matrix element on the
magnetic quantum numbers is pure geometry. This is the Wigner–Eckart theorem,

⟨j′m′∣Tqk∣jm⟩=(−1)j′−m′(j′kj−m′qm)⟨j′∥Tk∥j⟩=⟨jm kq∣j′m′⟩2j′+1 ⟨j′∥Tk∥j⟩.(M3.24)\langle j'm'|T^k_q|jm\rangle = (-1)^{j'-m'}\begin{pmatrix}j' & k & j\\ -m' & q & m\end{pmatrix}\langle j'\|T^k\|j\rangle = \frac{\langle jm\,kq|j'm'\rangle}{\sqrt{2j'+1}}\,\langle j'\|T^k\|j\rangle . \tag{M3.24} ⟨j′m′∣Tqk​∣jm⟩=(−1)j′−m′(j′−m′​kq​jm​)⟨j′∥Tk∥j⟩=2j′+1​⟨jmkq∣j′m′⟩​⟨j′∥Tk∥j⟩.(M3.24)

The two forms are equal for integer kkk. The idea of the proof is that, by (M3.23), Tqk∣jm⟩T^k_q|jm\rangleTqk​∣jm⟩
transforms under rotations exactly like the product state ∣kq⟩∣jm⟩|kq\rangle|jm\rangle∣kq⟩∣jm⟩. Its components can
therefore be combined with Clebsch–Gordan coefficients into vectors that behave like ∣j′m′⟩|j'm'\rangle∣j′m′⟩, and
the overlap of ⟨j′m′∣\langle j'm'|⟨j′m′∣ with such a vector cannot depend on m′m'm′, for the same reason that all
members of a multiplet have the same norm (derivation D.2). All the physics is in one number, the
reduced matrix element ⟨j′∥Tk∥j⟩\langle j'\|T^k\|j\rangle⟨j′∥Tk∥j⟩. The 3j symbol carries the selection rules:
m′=m+qm' = m + qm′=m+q and the triangle ∣j−k∣≤j′≤j+k|j - k| \le j' \le j + k∣j−k∣≤j′≤j+k. A tensor of rank kkk “carries” angular momentum
kkk, and its matrix elements behave like the Clebsch–Gordan coefficients for adding kkk to jjj.

Conventions. (M3.24) follows Edmonds (1957) and Bohr & Mottelson, as do these notes. Other
books absorb the factor 1/2j′+11/\sqrt{2j'+1}1/2j′+1​ into the reduced matrix element, or use a different phase.
Formulas that contain reduced matrix elements, such as B(Eλ)B(E\lambda)B(Eλ) below, then change by such
factors. Always check the convention of a table or a code before using its numbers.

For spherical harmonics, the integral of three of them (the Gaunt integral) gives the reduced
matrix element directly:

∫Yl1m1Yl2m2Yl3m3 dΩ=(2l1+1)(2l2+1)(2l3+1)4π(l1l2l3000)(l1l2l3m1m2m3),⟨l′∥Yλ∥l⟩=(−1)l′(2l′+1)(2λ+1)(2l+1)4π(l′λl000).(M3.25)\int Y_{l_1m_1}Y_{l_2m_2}Y_{l_3m_3}\,d\Omega = \sqrt{\frac{(2l_1+1)(2l_2+1)(2l_3+1)}{4\pi}} \begin{pmatrix}l_1 & l_2 & l_3\\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}l_1 & l_2 & l_3\\ m_1 & m_2 & m_3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \langle l'\|Y_\lambda\|l\rangle = (-1)^{l'}\sqrt{\frac{(2l'+1)(2\lambda+1)(2l+1)}{4\pi}} \begin{pmatrix}l' & \lambda & l\\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{M3.25} ∫Yl1​m1​​Yl2​m2​​Yl3​m3​​dΩ=4π(2l1​+1)(2l2​+1)(2l3​+1)​​(l1​0​l2​0​l3​0​)(l1​m1​​l2​m2​​l3​m3​​),⟨l′∥Yλ​∥l⟩=(−1)l′4π(2l′+1)(2λ+1)(2l+1)​​(l′0​λ0​l0​).(M3.25)

The first form follows from the way products of rotation matrices decompose, together with (M3.20);
the second from comparing the first with (M3.24) (derivation D.3). Reversing the signs of all mmm does
nothing to a 3j symbol whose mmm all vanish, yet multiplies it by (−1)l1+l2+l3(-1)^{l_1+l_2+l_3}(−1)l1​+l2​+l3​, so that symbol is zero
unless l1+l2+l3l_1 + l_2 + l_3l1​+l2​+l3​ is even. This is parity again: a multipole YλY_\lambdaYλ​ connects lll and l′l'l′ only if
l+λ+l′l + \lambda + l'l+λ+l′ is even.

Fig. M3.5 tests the theorem the hard way. All 29 matrix elements ⟨3m′∣Y2q∣3m⟩\langle 3m'|Y_{2q}|3m\rangle⟨3m′∣Y2q​∣3m⟩ are
computed by numerical quadrature on the sphere. Divided by the geometric factor of (M3.24), the 27
with a non-zero 3j symbol all give the same number, −0.861813824304-0.861813824304−0.861813824304, to 4×10−144\times10^{-14}4×10−14. That is
⟨3∥Y2∥3⟩\langle 3\|Y_2\|3\rangle⟨3∥Y2​∥3⟩ from (M3.25). The other two matrix elements vanish, as the theorem
requires.

The theorem has an immediate application to deformed nuclei. The intrinsic quadrupole moment Q0Q_0Q0​
describes the shape (M3.21) in its own frame. The quadrupole moment measured in the laboratory, the
spectroscopic quadrupole moment Qs(I)=⟨I,M=I∣Q20∣I,M=I⟩Q_s(I) = \langle I,M{=}I|Q_{20}|I,M{=}I\rangleQs​(I)=⟨I,M=I∣Q20​∣I,M=I⟩, is smaller,

integral over ∣YII∣2|Y_{II}|^2∣YII​∣2 (derivation D.4), gives

Qs(I)=−I2I+3 Q0.(M3.26)Q_s(I) = -\frac{I}{2I+3}\,Q_0 . \tag{M3.26} Qs​(I)=−2I+3I​Q0​.(M3.26)

For I=2I = 2I=2, Qs=−27Q0Q_s = -\frac27Q_0Qs​=−72​Q0​: a prolate nucleus (Q0>0Q_0 > 0Q0​>0) shows a negative quadrupole moment in
its 2⁺ state. The sign has a simple picture. In the state M=IM = IM=I the angular momentum points along zzz,
and the symmetry axis of a K=0K = 0K=0 rotor, which is perpendicular to the angular momentum, lies mostly

I=2,4,6I = 2, 4, 6I=2,4,6 by quadrature and by (M3.24).

B(Eλ; Ii→If)=∣⟨If∥M(Eλ)∥Ii⟩∣22Ii+1,B(E2; 0+→2+)=516π e2Q02(K=0),(M3.27)B(E\lambda;\,I_i \to I_f) = \frac{|\langle I_f\|\mathcal M(E\lambda)\|I_i\rangle|^2}{2I_i + 1},\qquad B(E2;\,0^+ \to 2^+) = \frac{5}{16\pi}\,e^2Q_0^2 \quad (K = 0), \tag{M3.27} B(Eλ;Ii​→If​)=2Ii​+1∣⟨If​∥M(Eλ)∥Ii​⟩∣2​,B(E2;0+→2+)=16π5​e2Q02​(K=0),(M3.27)

with M(Eλ,μ)=∑pe rpλYλμ(r^p)\mathcal M(E\lambda, \mu) = \sum_p e\,r_p^\lambda Y_{\lambda\mu}(\hat{\mathbf r}_p)M(Eλ,μ)=∑p​erpλ​Yλμ​(r^p​) summed over the

β2=4π3ZR02B(E2) ⁣↑e2.(M3.28)\beta_2 = \frac{4\pi}{3ZR_0^2}\sqrt{\frac{B(E2)\!\uparrow}{e^2}} . \tag{M3.28} β2​=3ZR02​4π​e2B(E2)↑​​.(M3.28)

M3.8 Recoupling: 6j and 9j symbols

Many problems involve more than two angular momenta: a projectile spin, an orbit and a target spin, or
two nucleons, each with an orbit and a spin. Three angular momenta can be coupled to a total JJJ in
different orders: (j1j2)J12(j_1j_2)J_{12}(j1​j2​)J12​ first and then j3j_3j3​, or (j2j3)J23(j_2j_3)J_{23}(j2​j3​)J23​ first and then j1j_1j1​. Both orders
give orthonormal bases. The transformation between them depends only on angular momenta, not on any
mmm, and defines the Wigner 6j symbol:

⟨(j1j2)J12, j3; J ∣ j1, (j2j3)J23; J⟩=(−1)j1+j2+j3+J(2J12+1)(2J23+1){j1j2J12j3JJ23}.(M3.29)\big\langle (j_1j_2)J_{12},\,j_3;\,J\,\big|\,j_1,\,(j_2j_3)J_{23};\,J\big\rangle = (-1)^{j_1+j_2+j_3+J}\sqrt{(2J_{12}+1)(2J_{23}+1)} \begin{Bmatrix}j_1 & j_2 & J_{12}\\ j_3 & J & J_{23}\end{Bmatrix}. \tag{M3.29} ⟨(j1​j2​)J12​,j3​;J∣∣∣​j1​,(j2​j3​)J23​;J⟩=(−1)j1​+j2​+j3​+J(2J12​+1)(2J23​+1)​{j1​j3​​j2​J​J12​J23​​}.(M3.29)

To compute the overlap, expand both states in product states with (M3.9). It becomes a sum, over all
magnetic quantum numbers, of products of four Clebsch–Gordan coefficients, one for each coupling. The
sum does not depend on MMM, for the same reason as in the Wigner–Eckart theorem: both states belong to
multiplets with the same JJJ, on which J±J_\pmJ±​ act in the same way. A 6j symbol vanishes unless its four
triads (j1j2J12)(j_1j_2J_{12})(j1​j2​J12​), (j1JJ23)(j_1JJ_{23})(j1​JJ23​), (j3j2J23)(j_3j_2J_{23})(j3​j2​J23​) and (j3JJ12)(j_3JJ_{12})(j3​JJ12​) satisfy the triangle rule, one for
each of the four couplings. It is invariant under any permutation of its columns and under exchanging
the upper and lower entries in any two columns. Because (M3.29) is an orthogonal transformation,

∑J12(2J12+1)(2J23+1){j1j2J12j3JJ23}{j1j2J12j3JJ23′}=δJ23J23′.(M3.30)\sum_{J_{12}}(2J_{12}+1)(2J_{23}+1) \begin{Bmatrix}j_1 & j_2 & J_{12}\\ j_3 & J & J_{23}\end{Bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix}j_1 & j_2 & J_{12}\\ j_3 & J & J'_{23}\end{Bmatrix} = \delta_{J_{23}J'_{23}} . \tag{M3.30} J12​∑​(2J12​+1)(2J23​+1){j1​j3​​j2​J​J12​J23​​}{j1​j3​​j2​J​J12​J23′​​}=δJ23​J23′​​.(M3.30)

Racah’s formula for the 6j symbol is again an alternating sum of factorials, and scatlib.angmom
again evaluates it exactly.

The choice of coupling order is not academic in reaction theory. A projectile of spin sss in an orbit
lll about a target of spin III can be coupled in two standard ways (§M3.9). The channel-spin order
couples S=s⊕IS = s \oplus IS=s⊕I first and then J=l⊕SJ = l \oplus SJ=l⊕S. The order used by FRESCO couples j=l⊕sj = l \oplus sj=l⊕s
first and then J=j⊕IJ = j \oplus IJ=j⊕I. By (M3.29), with j1=lj_1 = lj1​=l, j2=sj_2 = sj2​=s and j3=Ij_3 = Ij3​=I,

⟨(ls)j, I; J ∣ l, (sI)S; J⟩=(−1)l+s+I+J(2j+1)(2S+1){lsjIJS}.(M3.31)\big\langle (ls)j,\,I;\,J\,\big|\,l,\,(sI)S;\,J\big\rangle = (-1)^{l+s+I+J}\sqrt{(2j+1)(2S+1)}\begin{Bmatrix}l & s & j\\ I & J & S\end{Bmatrix}. \tag{M3.31} ⟨(ls)j,I;J∣∣∣​l,(sI)S;J⟩=(−1)l+s+I+J(2j+1)(2S+1)​{lI​sJ​jS​}.(M3.31)

For l=2l = 2l=2, s=12s = \frac12s=21​, I=32I = \frac32I=23​ and J=2J = 2J=2, the notebook gets the 2×22\times22×2 matrix with
rows j=32,52j = \frac32, \frac52j=23​,25​ and columns S=1,2S = 1, 2S=1,2:
(−0.5480.8370.8370.548)\begin{pmatrix}-0.548 & 0.837\\ 0.837 & 0.548\end{pmatrix}(−0.5480.837​0.8370.548​). It agrees to 10−1610^{-16}10−16 with the overlaps
of the two bases built explicitly from Clebsch–Gordan coefficients. Cross sections do not depend on
the order, but SSS-matrix elements quoted by different codes do.

With four angular momenta the recoupling coefficients become 9j symbols. Their main use is the
transformation from LSLSLS coupling (orbital angular momenta coupled to LLL, spins to SSS) to jjjjjj coupling
(each particle’s lll and sss coupled to jjj):

⟨(l1s1)j1, (l2s2)j2; J ∣ (l1l2)L, (s1s2)S; J⟩=(2j1+1)(2j2+1)(2L+1)(2S+1){l1s1j1l2s2j2LSJ},(M3.32)\big\langle (l_1s_1)j_1,\,(l_2s_2)j_2;\,J\,\big|\,(l_1l_2)L,\,(s_1s_2)S;\,J\big\rangle = \sqrt{(2j_1+1)(2j_2+1)(2L+1)(2S+1)} \begin{Bmatrix}l_1 & s_1 & j_1\\ l_2 & s_2 & j_2\\ L & S & J\end{Bmatrix}, \tag{M3.32} ⟨(l1​s1​)j1​,(l2​s2​)j2​;J∣∣∣​(l1​l2​)L,(s1​s2​)S;J⟩=(2j1​+1)(2j2​+1)(2L+1)(2S+1)​⎩⎪⎨⎪⎧​l1​l2​L​s1​s2​S​j1​j2​J​⎭⎪⎬⎪⎫​,(M3.32)

and a 9j symbol is computed as a sum over products of three 6j symbols:

The most important application in reaction theory is the matrix element of a scalar product of two

V(r,θ′)=∑λVλ(r) Yλ0(θ′)=∑λVλ(r) 4π2λ+1  Yλ(r^)⋅Yλ(e^).(M3.35)V(r, \theta') = \sum_\lambda V_\lambda(r)\,Y_{\lambda0}(\theta') = \sum_\lambda V_\lambda(r)\,\sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{2\lambda+1}}\;Y_\lambda(\hat{\mathbf r})\cdot Y_\lambda(\hat{\mathbf e}) . \tag{M3.35} V(r,θ′)=λ∑​Vλ​(r)Yλ0​(θ′)=λ∑​Vλ​(r)2λ+14π​​Yλ​(r^)⋅Yλ​(e^).(M3.35)

M3.9 Counting coupled channels

The tools are now complete, and we can assemble the basis of a coupled-channels calculation. A
channel specifies the internal states of the two nuclei (spins sss and III, parities πa\pi_aπa​ and
πA\pi_AπA​), the orbital angular momentum lll of their relative motion, and how the three are coupled. The
total angular momentum JJJ, its projection MMM and the parity are conserved. Parity is multiplicative:
the intrinsic parities of the two nuclei times the parity (−1)l(-1)^l(−1)l of the relative motion (§M3.2),

π=πa πA (−1)l.(M3.36)\pi = \pi_a\,\pi_A\,(-1)^l . \tag{M3.36} π=πa​πA​(−1)l.(M3.36)

The coupled-channel equations therefore split into independent sets, one for each JπJ^\piJπ. Listing
the channels in a set is a matter of the triangle rule and (M3.36). scatlib.angmom.channels does it in
both coupling orders of §M3.8; the counts always agree.

Three examples from the notebook show how this works. For α + ²⁰Ne with the 0⁺, 2⁺, 4⁺ band,
Jπ=0+J^\pi = 0^+Jπ=0+ has 3 channels, (0+,l=0)(0^+, l{=}0)(0+,l=0), (2+,2)(2^+, 2)(2+,2) and (4+,4)(4^+, 4)(4+,4), because each state III must combine
with l=Il = Il=I to give J=0J = 0J=0. Jπ=2+J^\pi = 2^+Jπ=2+ has 7. From J=4J = 4J=4 on, every natural-parity set,
π=(−1)J\pi = (-1)^Jπ=(−1)J, has 9 channels. Unnatural-parity sets, such as 1+1^+1+ with 2 channels or Jπ=10−J^\pi = 10^-Jπ=10− with
6, also exist. But the entrance channel, α plus ²⁰Ne in its 0⁺ ground state, has π=(−1)l=(−1)J\pi = (-1)^l = (-1)^Jπ=(−1)l=(−1)J,
so they are never populated. For p + ¹²C with the 0⁺ and 2⁺ states, Jπ=32+J^\pi = \frac32^+Jπ=23​+ has 5 channels,
for instance (0+,l=2,S=12)(0^+, l{=}2, S{=}\frac12)(0+,l=2,S=21​) in the channel-spin order, or (0+,l=2,j=32)(0^+, l{=}2, j{=}\frac32)(0+,l=2,j=23​) in
FRESCO’s. The simplest case is spin ½ on a spin-0 target with no excited states. For each JJJ there
are two channels, l=J±12l = J \pm \frac12l=J±21​, but they have opposite parity, so each JπJ^\piJπ set has a single
channel. This is why the phase shifts δl±\delta_l^\pmδl±​ of Chapter 6 do not mix.

The number of channels grows quickly with the number of excited states. For a K=0K = 0K=0 band
0+,2+,…,Imax⁡0^+, 2^+, \dots, I_{\max}0+,2+,…,Imax​ and natural parity with J≥Imax⁡J \ge I_{\max}J≥Imax​, the state III contributes the I+1I + 1I+1
values l=J−I,J−I+2,…,J+Il = J - I, J - I + 2, \dots, J + Il=J−I,J−I+2,…,J+I. The number of channels per JJJ is therefore

Nch=∑I=0,2,…Imax⁡(I+1)=(Imax⁡2+1)2,(M3.37)N_{\rm ch} = \sum_{I = 0, 2, \dots}^{I_{\max}}(I + 1) = \Big(\frac{I_{\max}}{2} + 1\Big)^2 , \tag{M3.37} Nch​=I=0,2,…∑Imax​​(I+1)=(2Imax​​+1)2,(M3.37)

that is 9 for the α + ²⁰Ne band and 49 for a band up to 12⁺ (Fig. M3.7). The work of solving coupled
equations grows like Nch3N_{\rm ch}^3Nch3​. The iso-centrifugal approximation of CCFULL (Chapter 14)
replaces the centrifugal barrier of every channel by that of the entrance channel. The algebra then
decouples, and only one channel per intrinsic state remains: 7 instead of 49, a factor of 343 in work.
For heavy-ion fusion, where many partial waves and many excited states contribute, this is what
makes realistic calculations cheap.

unnatural parity, and the three channels of the iso-centrifugal approximation (dashed).
(b) Channels per natural-parity JJJ (J≥Imax⁡J \ge I_{\max}J≥Imax​) for a K=0K = 0K=0 band 0+,2+,…,Imax⁡0^+, 2^+, \dots, I_{\max}0+,2+,…,Imax​:
all channels (M3.37) and the iso-centrifugal count (dashed). (Notebook §M3.9.)

Summary

The commutation relations alone fix the spectrum of every angular momentum: the ladder operators step
mmm up and down, the requirement that their norms stay non-negative stops the ladder at ±j\pm j±j, and so
J2\mathbf J^2J2 takes the values j(j+1)j(j+1)j(j+1) with 2j2j2j an integer, with the matrix elements (M3.3) in the
Condon–Shortley phase. Orbital angular momentum is restricted to integers by single-valuedness, so
half-integers come only from spin, and an angular momentum never points exactly along an axis. Spin ½
is described by the Pauli matrices, and a rotation by 2π2\pi2π changes the sign of a spinor. Two angular
momenta are combined with Clebsch–Gordan coefficients, constructed by the ladder operators and
orthogonality and tabulated as 3j symbols; they obey the triangle rule and, for large quantum numbers,
oscillate about the probability distribution of the classical vector model. Coupling spin and orbit
gives ⟨l⋅s⟩=l/2\langle\mathbf l\cdot\mathbf s\rangle = l/2⟨l⋅s⟩=l/2 or −(l+1)/2-(l+1)/2−(l+1)/2, and the strong, surface-peaked nuclear spin–orbit
force pulls the high-jjj levels into the shell below and produces the magic numbers 28, 50, 82 and
126; for ²⁰⁸Pb the computed N=126N = 126N=126 gap, 3.55 MeV, compares with 3.43 MeV measured. Rotations mix mmm
but never jjj, through the DDD-matrices, of which Dm0lD^l_{m0}Dm0l​ is a spherical harmonic and DM0ID^I_{M0}DM0I​ the wave
function of a rotating K=0K = 0K=0 nucleus. The Wigner–Eckart theorem separates geometry, a 3j symbol, from
physics, a reduced matrix element, because a tensor operator acting on a state transforms like a
coupled pair of angular momenta; it yields the selection rules, Qs=−I2I+3Q0Q_s = -\frac{I}{2I+3}Q_0Qs​=−2I+3I​Q0​ and the relation
between B(E2)B(E2)B(E2) and β2\beta_2β2​. Three and four angular momenta are recoupled with 6j and 9j symbols, which
give the transformations between coupling schemes and, through (M3.34), the coupling matrix of a
deformed potential in the channel basis. Finally, channels are grouped by JπJ^\piJπ; from a 0⁺ + 0⁺
entrance channel only natural parity is reached, and the number of channels grows so quickly with the
number of excited states that approximations such as the iso-centrifugal one become essential.

Detailed derivation

Several results above were derived only in outline, so as not to interrupt the argument. This section
gives the complete algebra, in the order in which the results appear in the chapter.

D.2 The Wigner–Eckart theorem

The second form of (M3.23) says that the commutators of J\mathbf JJ with TqkT^k_qTqk​ are the matrix elements of
J\mathbf JJ for angular momentum kkk. Consequently J\mathbf JJ acts on the vectors Tqk∣jm⟩T^k_q|jm\rangleTqk​∣jm⟩ exactly as
j1+j2\mathbf j_1 + \mathbf j_2j1​+j2​ acts on product states ∣jm⟩∣kq⟩|jm\rangle|kq\rangle∣jm⟩∣kq⟩:
J Tqk∣jm⟩=[J,Tqk] ∣jm⟩+Tqk J∣jm⟩\mathbf J\,T^k_q|jm\rangle = [\mathbf J, T^k_q]\,|jm\rangle + T^k_q\,\mathbf J|jm\rangleJTqk​∣jm⟩=[J,Tqk​]∣jm⟩+Tqk​J∣jm⟩, where the first term changes qqq
as j2j_{2}j2​ would and the second changes mmm as j1j_{1}j1​ would. Now form, for each J′′J''J′′ and M′′M''M′′, the
combinations

∣J′′M′′⟩ ⁣⟩=∑m,q⟨jm kq∣J′′M′′⟩ Tqk∣jm⟩.|J''M''\rangle\!\rangle = \sum_{m,q}\langle jm\,kq|J''M''\rangle\,T^k_q|jm\rangle . ∣J′′M′′⟩⟩=m,q∑​⟨jmkq∣J′′M′′⟩Tqk​∣jm⟩.

The construction of §M3.4 used only the action of the two angular momenta on the product states, so it
applies here unchanged: Jz∣J′′M′′⟩ ⁣⟩=M′′∣J′′M′′⟩ ⁣⟩J_z|J''M''\rangle\!\rangle = M''|J''M''\rangle\!\rangleJz​∣J′′M′′⟩⟩=M′′∣J′′M′′⟩⟩ and
J±∣J′′M′′⟩ ⁣⟩=J′′(J′′+1)−M′′(M′′±1)  ∣J′′,M′′±1⟩ ⁣⟩J_\pm|J''M''\rangle\!\rangle = \sqrt{J''(J''+1) - M''(M''\pm1)}\;|J'', M''\pm1\rangle\!\rangleJ±​∣J′′M′′⟩⟩=J′′(J′′+1)−M′′(M′′±1)​∣J′′,M′′±1⟩⟩, and therefore also
J2=J−J++Jz2+Jz\mathbf J^2 = J_-J_+ + J_z^2 + J_zJ2=J−​J+​+Jz2​+Jz​ acts on them as J′′(J′′+1)J''(J''+1)J′′(J′′+1). The vectors ∣J′′M′′⟩ ⁣⟩|J''M''\rangle\!\rangle∣J′′M′′⟩⟩ need not be
normalized, and some may vanish, but they behave like eigenstates of J2\mathbf J^2J2 and JzJ_zJz​.

Take the overlap with an eigenstate ⟨j′m′∣\langle j'm'|⟨j′m′∣. It vanishes unless j′=J′′j' = J''j′=J′′ and m′=M′′m' = M''m′=M′′, because
eigenvectors of the Hermitian operators J2\mathbf J^2J2 and JzJ_zJz​ with different eigenvalues are orthogonal. It
